1

INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE
I am David A. Robinson, age 73 , a Connecticut
lawyer.1 I am the amicus and counsel for the amicus.
My interest in this case stems from my effort in 2023-
24 to start a movement to amend the Second
Amendment for modern times and modern safety
needs. I wrote a short book, Amending the
Constitution to Reduce Gun Violence , and self -
published it on Amazon (Kindle Direct Publishing) . I
drafted a constitutional amendment, inserted it in the
book, and posted the amendment on Amazon so
people can read the amendment without having to
buy the book.  The book and amendment remain on
Amazon today.
I wrote the book and amendment because District
of Columbia v. Heller, 544 U.S. 570, 636 (2008), states
“it is not the role of this Court to pronounce the
Second Amendment extinct.” Heller thus implies that
it is the role of the American people to pronounce the
Second Amendment extinct or partly extinct.  The
American people can pass a constitutional
amendment clarifying or repealing the Second.

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part.
No counsel or party or anyone else made a monetary contribution
to fund the preparation or submission of this brief. I wrote and
paid for it entirely myself.

2

Someone needs to start the process, so I started it. In
sections I and VII infra, I tell briefly about my effort.
My effort was largely a failure , for reasons I explain
in section VII . Those reasons indicate that it is  the
role of this Court to pronounce the Second extinct or
partly extinct. This Court cannot expect the American
people to do so.
In sections II through VI, and VIII, I explain why
the Second Amendment does not  give civilians the
right to semiautomatic weapons including the AR-15.
Also in section VIII, I illustrate why the First, Third,
Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth
Amendments fully apply today but the Second only
partly applies today.
My interest also stems from my residing in
Connecticut. Connecticut is a respondent in this case.
I want Connecticut’s law on AR-15s to remain in force.
I practiced law in Massachusetts from 1977 to
2008, then moved to Connecticut. I earned my J.D. in
1977 from Washington University in St. Louis. I am
admitted to practice in the United States Supreme
Court.

3


SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
This Court should pronounce what is and is not
extinct about the Second Amendment. I tried to start
a movement to pass a constitutional amendment—the
28th Amendment ---to pronounce what is and is not
extinct about the Second but was unable to persuade
a majority to agree on the wording of the 28th. Based
on my experience, this Court should not expect the
American people to do so. The Second Amendment is
not extinct in toto  but the prefatory clause (“A well
regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a
free State”) is extinct, so the operative clause (“the
right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not
be infringed”) is extinct unless the right is inherent.
The right to self -defense is inherent, so the Second
Amendment gives civilians the right to keep and bear
arms for self-defense. If some people believe that their
local, state, or federal government is tyrannical, that
does not give those people the right to shoot
government officials or possess an AR -15. Capacity
limits on firearms are analogous to speed limits on
cars: The limits are constitutional and protect public
safety.

4

ARGUMENT
I.  Th e Court should pronounce  what is ,
and is not , extinct about the Second
Amendment. The Court should not expect
the American people to do so. I tried to
start a movement to persuade the
American people to amend the
Constitution to clarify the Second
Amendment for modern times , but I failed
because t he people cannot agree on the
language of an amendment clarifying the
Second.
The Court opined in District of Columbia v.
Heller, 544 U.S. 570, 636 (2008), that “it is not the role
of this Court to pronounce the Second Amendment
extinct.” If it is not the role of this Court, whose role
is it? Heller implies that it is the role of the American
people. The American people can pass a constitutional
amendment clarifying or repealing the Second
Amendment for modern times . The people would, I
assume, need to pass a 28th Amendment to the
Constitution to do that.
To pass a constitutional amendment, someone
must draft an amendment and start the process set
forth in Constitution article V. Unaware of anyone
else proposing to amend the Constitution to clarify or

5

repeal the Second, I proposed an amendment myself.
I drafted an amendment and wrote a short book about
it. Later in this brief I will discuss it but I will say
right now that my effort was unsuccessful. One
reason it was unsuccessful is that people cannot agree
on what the new amendment should say. Therefore,
it is the role of this Court to pronounce what is, and is
not, extinct about the Second Amendment. This Court
should not expect the American people to do so.
II. The Second Amendment is not extinct in
toto but the prefatory clause (“A well
regulated Militia, being necessary to the
security of a free State ”) is extinct, so the
operative clause (“the right of the people to
keep and bear Arms, shall not be
infringed”) is extinct unless the right is
inherent. The right to self -defense is
inherent, so the Second Amendment gives
civilians the right to keep and bear arms
necessary for self-defense.
The prefatory clause of the Second Amendment—
“A well regulated militia, being necessary to the
security of a free State” —means that the Second
Amendment gives government the authority to ban or
limit possession of arms by people not  in the militia.
District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 637, 643,
681 (2008) (Stevens and Breyer, JJ., dissenting).

6

People not in the militia are civilians. Nicely v. United
States, 23 F.4th 1364, 1369 (Fed. Cir. 2022) (“civilian”
is “person who is not on active duty in the armed
services”). Had our Founding Fathers wanted every
civilian to have the right to a gun, the Second
Amendment would read simply, “The right of the
people to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed.”
The second Militia Act of 1792, § 1 (May 8, 1792),
commanded militiamen to provide themselves with “a
good musket or firelock” and either 24 cartridges or
20 balls suited to the bore of the musket, firelock, or
rifle. When the Court in United States v. Miller, 307
U.S. 174, 181 -82 (1939), said militiamen were
expected to bear arms of the kind in common use “at
the time," the Court meant 1792, not 1939 and
certainly not 2026. “This Court normally interprets a
statute in accord with the ordinary public meaning of
its terms at the time of its enactment,” Bostock v.
Clayton County , 590 U.S. 644, 654 (2020), and
interprets constitutional amendments likewise.
Fulton v. City of Philadelphia , 593 U.S. 522, 570- 71
(2021) (Alito, J., concurring).
That does not mean the Second Amendment
protects only arms in existence in the 18th century.
The Second Amendment protects 21st century arms
to the extent necessary for self -defense. “[I]ndividual
self-defense is the central component of the Second
Amendment right." New York State Rifle & Pistol

7

Assn, Inc. v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1, 29 (2022) ( citation
modified). “[T]he inherent right of self- defense has
been central to the Second Amendment right.”
District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. at 628. The
Court repeated this twice in June 2026. On June 18
the Court held, “The Second Amendment protects the
right of all Americans to keep and bear firearms for
self-defense.” United States v. Hemani , 146 S. Ct.
1677, 1685 (citation modified). On June 25 the Court
held, “The Second and Fourteenth Amendments
protect the right to carry handguns inside or outside
the home for self -defense.” Wolford v. Lopez , 146 S.
Ct. 2032, 2040. Had someone told our Founding
Fathers in 1791 that 235 years later there will be a
firearm enabling an individual to kill 60 people in 60
seconds, I believe they would have worded the Second
Amendment to not give a civilian the right to such a
high-capacity firearm.
In Garland v. Cargill , 602 U.S. 406 (2024), the
Court held that bump -stocked semiautomatic
weapons are not “machine guns,” and thus the
prohibition against “machine guns” in the National
Firearms Act of 1934  does not apply. Nowhere in
Garland did the Court mention the Second
Amendment. Thus, bump -stocked semiautomatic
weapons are not a Second Amendment right.
Congress can ban them. 602 U.S. at 429 (Alito, J. ,

8

concurring). Congress and/or a state can ban
semiautomatic weapons in general.
In my book I come up with an analogy, which I
will tell in the next section of this brief, that I believe
proves that the Second and Fourteenth Amendments
do not guarantee civilians the right to keep and bear
semiautomatic rifles in common use in 2026 including
the AR- 15. Many civilians have that right anyway
and will continue to, regardless of the Court’s decision
in this case, because many states give civilians that
right. Those states, not the Second and Fourteenth
Amendments, give them that right. United States v.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 737 (2024) (Barrett, J. ,
concurring) (“That evidence marks where the [Second
Amendment] right stops and the State's authority to
regulate begins.”). Congress could, according to the
Commerce Clause, U.S. Const. art . 1, § 8, cl. 3, g ive
civilians that right in all 50 states but has not done
so. Connecticut does not give civilians that right.
Connecticut bans semiautomatic rifles including the
AR-15.
The Court should rule on semiautomatic
weaponry the way the Court ruled on abortion: It is
not a constitutional right, but if Congress and/or
states want to allow it, they can allow it. Dobbs v.
Jackson Women's Health Org., 597 U.S. 215 (2022).

9

III. The Second Amendment’s “militia”
clause is analogous to Major League
Baseball’s pre-1947 “Whites only” policy: It
made sense to most Americans at the time
but makes no sense today.
The Second Amendment is unique: It is the only
provision in our Constitution with a prefatory clause.
Heller, 554 U.S. at 577. If the prefatory clause no
longer applies, the operative clause—“The right of the
people to keep and bear arms, shall not be
infringed”—no longer applies unless there is
indication elsewhere in the Constitution that the
operative clause applies. I believe there is such
indication. I believe, and Heller holds, that the right
to be armed for self -defense is “ancient” and
“inherent.” Id. at 594, 599, 628. So, the holdings in
Heller and Bruen that a person has the right to keep
and carry a handgun for self-defense make sense. The
argument that the Second Amendment’s “militia”
clause gives a civilian the right to an AR-15 makes no
sense.
The Second Amendment is analogous to the
“gentlemen’s agreement” in Major League Baseball
(MLB) from 1901 to 1947 regarding Black ballplayers.
Had the “agreement” been written, it may have read,
“An all -White team being necessary to maximize
Major League B aseball’s popularity and the number
of people who attend MLB games, the right of the

10

teams to hire only White ballplayers shall not be
infringed.” As absurd and hateful as such an
agreement sounds in 2026, it made sense to most
White Americans then, especially in the MLB cities
and surrounding areas  then. From 1901 to 1947 no
MLB team was south of Washington, DC, or St. Louis,
MO. A supermajority of Americans in the N ortheast
and Upper Midwest, where all 16 MLB teams played,
were White. Most Blacks lived in the South. American
society was segregated. Black ballplayers had their
own leagues, called “Negro Leagues,” so did not need
to play “major” league (American or National League)
baseball. In 1947 the Brooklyn Dodgers and Jackie
Robinson (no relation to me) broke the color barrier in
MLB. Invoking the 1791 “militia” clause to give
civilians in 2026 the right to a rifle enabling a civilian
to kill 60 people in 60 seconds is analogous to a
baseball team’s invoking the 1901 to 1947
“gentlemen’s agreement” in 2026 to hire Whites only.
Whatever sense, if any, the prefatory clause made in
1791 or 1901, the preface is “outmoded” and “extinct”
in the 21st century, to borrow words from Heller, 554
U.S. at 636. The preface is no longer the basis of the
operative clause, so the standalone operative clause
should be limited to self-defense.

11

IV. No American has been drafted (forced)
into military service since 1973. The
Selective Service System has replaced the
“militia.” The “militia” is essentially
extinct and thus cannot be the basis of gun
rights today.
The “militia” exists today on paper but most gun
owners are not in it, and the Selective Service System
has essentially replaced it. According to 10 U.S.C. §
246, the “militia” consists only of 1) able-bodied males
ages 17 to 44, 2) military veterans ages 45 -64 who
enlist in the National Guard, and 3) female members
of the National Guard. Thus, reading the Second
Amendment in the light most favorable to AR -15
owners, only people in those three categories have a
Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms.
Connecticut likewise has a “militia” today on paper:
All male citizens  . . . between the ages of
eighteen and forty-five years, not exempt by
law, shall be subject to military duty and
designated as the militia. All female citizens
. . . between the ages of eighteen and forty -
five years, may enlist voluntarily in any
women's unit of the armed forces of the
state.
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 27-2.

12

No American since 1973 has been drafted (forced)
into military service. Barry M. Stentiford, Selective
Service Before the All-Volunteer Force, MILITARY REV.,
Nov.-Dec. 2023, at 114-15, 123. To my knowledge, no
state or local government has drafted (forced) anyone
into military service, that is, forced anyone to become
a state or local police officer, since long before 1973 if
ever. The federal, state, and local armed forces have
been all-volunteer since 1973 or earlier.
Suppose another nation attacks the United States
and there are not enough soldiers in the all-volunteer
U.S. Armed Forces to defend against the attack. Does
the United States need a way to quickly draft (force)
people into military service? Yes. That is wh y 10
U.S.C. § 246 remains in effect. That is why we have a
Selective Service System:
Federal law requires nearly all male U.S.
citizens and male immigrants to register at
age 18. . . .
In a national emergency, Selective Service
System will use the registry to provide
personnel to the Department of War and
alternative service for conscientious
objectors, if authorized by the President and
Congress.

13

https://www.sss.gov (last visited Oct. 22 , 2026). That
does not give a civilian the right to an AR -15. I still
carry my draft card (S elective Service System
Registration Certificate), issued February 8, 1971, in
my wallet because the card says I must have the card
in my “personal possession at all times and to
surrender it upon entering active duty in the Armed
Forces.” That does not give me the right to an AR -15
and never did.
V. If the Second Amendment gives people the
right to keep and bear AR -15s to defend
against a tyrannical government , who
decides if a government is tyrannical? Many
people today (October 2026) believe that their
local, state, or federal government is
tyrannical.
AR-15 owners assert that the Second
Amendment’s prefatory clause gives nearly everyone
the right to an AR -15. They assert they need the
ability to kill 60 people in 60 seconds or, at a
minimum, 20 people in 20 seconds. Why do they need
that ability? Becaus e, they assert, the Second
Amendment gives them the right to defend against a
tyrannical government. District of Columbia v. Heller,
554 U.S. 570, 598, 600, 608- 09 (2008). They believe
that a government that bans AR -15 rifles is
tyrannical. Id. at 608 -09, citing J. Story, A Familiar

14

Exposition of the Constitution of the United States §
450 (reprinted 1986). I assume —they can correct me
if I am mistaken—they therefore believe that if a law
enforcement officer in a state that bans AR -15 rifles
tries to seize an AR-15 or arrest or serve a warrant on
a person possessin g an AR- 15, the AR -15 possessor
has a Second Amendment right to shoot the
officer/tyrant. Since the officer/tyrant may have 19
officers/tyrants nearby as backup, an AR -15 is
necessary to shoot all 20. Their reasoning is circular:
The Second Amendment gives a civilian the right to
an AR-15 because if 20 cops try to seize  the civilian’s
AR-15, the civilian needs an AR -15 to shoot all 20. A
10-round pistol or 6 -round revolver won’t suffice.
They have a 1791 mentality and a 2026 AR -15—a
volatile combination.
VI. Capacity limits on rifles are analogous
to speed limits on c ars: They are
constitutional and protect public safety.
Travel is a constitutional right. Shapiro v.
Thompson, 394 U.S. 618, 629-30 (1969). Nevertheless,
the government has authority to impose speed limits
on automobiles. Likewise, the government has
authority to impose capacity limits on rifles. The fear
that many people have when AR -15s are legal is as
great as the fear people would have if there were no
speed limits.

15

VII. My proposed amendment says what
Heller and Bruen say and clarifies that the
Second Amendment today is for individual
self-defense, not “militia.”
Believing as I do that the Constitution should give
civilians the right to keep and bear arms for
individual self -defense, but fearing that this Court
might eventually hold that semiautomatic weapons
including the AR-15 are a Second Amendment right,
in 2023 I drafted an amendment —the 28th
Amendment to the U.S. Constitution—clarifying, not
repealing, the Second Amendment for modern times
and modern safety needs. I wrote and self-published
on Amazon (Kindle Direct Publishing) a very short
book (paperback is 29 pages) explaining it and the
amendment process , Amending the Constitution to
Reduce Gun Violence. I posted the amendment on the
book’s Amazon description page so anyone can read
the amendment without having to buy the book. Here
is, or was, my proposed amendment:
a. My Proposed 28th Amendment
to the United States Constitution
This amendment clarifies the Second
Amendment. People have a right to defend
themselves against physical harm. People have
the right to keep and bear arms to the extent
necessary to defend themselves, their families,

16

their homes, and other people nearby, and hunt
for food. Reasonable prohibitions on the owning,
possessing, and carrying of weapons by
criminals, the mentally ill, and people who have
unjustifiably threatened violence are lawful.
Owners of private property  may ban or restrict
the possession of arms on their property. The
Second Amendment does not restrict the
military’s use of arms and weaponry. The
military is the armed forces of the local, state,
and federal government. The right to defend
themselves against physical harm does not give
people the right to resist a lawful arrest by local,
state, or federal law enforcement officers.
Publicizing a book requires advertising. I paid
Amazon $5,300, all from my own pocket , from
February 2023 to March 2024 to advertise my book. I
created a slogan: “28 in 24. ” “Pass the 28th
Amendment in 2024 !” Word spread widely and
quickly (“viral ly”) among gun owners that a guy in
Connecticut (me) is proposing changes to the Second
Amendment. Gun owners posted negative reviews
and comments.
At the same time at the other end of the political
spectrum, many gun control  advocates opposed my
amendment. My proposed amendment declares that
nearly everyone has a Second Amendment right to a
gun. Gun control advocates hope this Court

17

eventually overrules Heller and Bruen and holds that
since the Second Amendment’s prefatory clause is
extinct, the operative clause is extinct, and therefore
no civilian has the right to a gun unless Congress or
the state government gives the civilian that right. My
amendment is a compromise between gun rights
advocates and gun control advocates.
I created a Facebook page , https://www.
facebook.com/NewSecondAmendment. I requested
and received Facebook’s permission to run political
Facebook ads. On March 23, 25, and 26, 2024, I paid
for and ran “28 in 24” Facebook ads. I don’t recall how
much I paid Facebook; my guess is around $1,000 but
I don’t remember precisely. It went viral. Gun owners
posted hundreds of negative comments while
hundreds of others  posted positive comments or
“likes.” Anyone on Facebook who wants to read them
can still read them today.
I emailed, by filling out the “contact me” form on
their office websites , my Congresswoman (Rosa
DeLauro), two U.S. Senators  (Richard Blumenthal
and Chris Murphy), President Joe Biden, and Vice
President Kamala Harris to ask them to propose my
amendment. I received from each a “thank you” but
no response to my specific proposal.
No one asked me or paid me to do any of this. I did
it on my own with my own money, as I stated above

18

and in footnote 1 of this brief. I am one man exercising
his First Amendment right to speak and petition the
government.
On July 29, 2025, I emailed President Donald
Trump (whitehouse.gov) and suggested that if he
wants to win the Nobel Peace Prize, he should propose
my proposed amendment. I received a “thank you” but
no response to my specific proposal. A lmost a year
later, on July 16, 2026, after this Court granted
certiorari in this case, I emailed President Trump and
suggested that if he wants to win the Nobel he should
cause the U.S. Department of Justice to file an amicus
brief in favor of the respondents in this case. On
September 4, the Justice Department filed an amicus
brief in favor of the petitioners.
If this Court rules in favor of the respondents, the
Court will essentially implement my proposed 28th
amendment. I respectfully request this Court to do so.
Someone needs to pronounce the Second Amendment
partly extinct. Someone needs to reduce the number
of mass shootings and the mass anxiety that some
people with semiautomatic weapons including the
AR-15 are causing . They are causing millions of
Americans to worry about mass shootings. A person
who goes to an outdoor concert is probably not worried
that a guy with a pistol or revolver will shoot a
concertgoer at random, but many people worry that a

19

guy with an AR -15 will shoot 30 concertgoers at
random.
VIII. A conversation with a 9-year-old
hiding in a c loset with her classmates and
teacher during a “lockdown” a/k/a “active
shooter” drill  at school illustrates that
semiautomatic firearms are not a Second
Amendment right.
The following hypothetical conversation between
a 9- year-old student (“Jane”) and her teacher while
both are hiding in a closet during  a “lockdown” or
“active shooter” drill proves that the Second
Amendment does not protect semiautomatic firearms.
Jane: “Why do we have to do this?”
Teacher: “We do it in case a man enter s the school
with a gun and tries to shoot all 29 of you and also
me. It would take him only 30 seconds. We have to
learn to hide and barricade ourselves quickly.”
Jane: “Can a gun shoot 30 people in 30 seconds?”
Teacher: “Guns don’t shoot people. People shoot
people. A gun is an inanimate object. It can’t do any
harm itself. Yes, a rifle called an AR-15 can enable
the rifleman to shoot 30 people in 30 seconds.”

20

Jane: “Why do they allow a gun like that? Why does
anyone need a gun like that?”
Teacher: “The Second Amendment to the U.S.
Constitution says you have the  right to keep and
bear arms and that no one can infringe on that
right. Guns are arms. Some people have AR-15s for
self-defense. Some have AR-15s to hunt animals for
food. Some have AR-15s because AR-15s are fun to
shoot.”
Jane: “We kids have to hide in a closet so grownups
can have fun?”
Teacher: “The Second Amendment says what it
says. It’s our constitutional right.”
Jane: “Can I have fun shooting an AR-15?”
Teacher. “No. You’re only 9. An AR -15 is a
dangerous weapon . It can shoot 30 people in 30
seconds. Only adults can shoot an AR-15.”
Jane: “I thought you said guns don’t shoot people.
May I read the Second Amendment?”
Teacher: “I’ll find it on my cellphone. Here it is.
Read it.”
Jane: “It says,  ‘A well regulated Militia, being
necessary to the security of a free State, the right

21

of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be
infringed.’ What’s a militia?”
Teacher: “When the United States was founded in
the 1780s and 1790s, we did not have a standing
professional army, so if foreigners or tyrants
attacked us, every man needed a rifle to shoot the
foreigners or tyrants. We called the men militia.”
Jane: “Do we have a militia today? Is my dad in it?
Are you in it?”
Teacher: “No.”
Jane: “Could the man with the gun in the 1790s
shoot 30 people in 30 seconds?”
Teacher: “No. The 1790s gun enabled him to shoot
only 2 people in 30 seconds.”
Jane: “Why would a man want to shoot 30 people
he doesn’t even know?”
Teacher: “Some men are angry at the world and
enjoy watching people suffer.”
Jane: “Can’t anyone help these men be happier? I
was angry once in class, so the teacher sent me to
the vice principal. The vice principal sent me to the
school nurse. The school nurse sent me to the
school guidance counselor. The school guidance

22

counselor sent me to the school psychologist. They
all tried to help me but I was still angry.”
Teacher: “You just answered your own question.
The mental health system doesn’t work very well.
Physical health is often visible or measurable.
Mental health is not. It is very difficult to know
what is inside a person’s mind.”
Jane: “Why does a man have the right to a gun
enabling him to shoot 30 people in 30 seconds when
a militia no longer exists and the militiaman’s gun
enabled him to shoot only 2 people in 30 seconds?”
That question—the last question Jane asked—is
the question presented in this case. Her conversation
with her teacher illustrates h ow the Second
Amendment is different from the First, Third, Fourth,
Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth amendments. Had
Jane asked about freedom of speech, freedom of
religion, quartering of soldiers, search and seizure,
probable cause, privilege against self -incrimination,
right to counsel, right to a speedy trial, right to jury
trial in criminal and civil cases, ban on excessive bail,
or ban on cruel and unusual punishment, the teacher
could show Jane the amendment and Jane would
understand where the right comes from. Reading the
Second Amendment, Jane cannot understand where
a civilian’s right to an AR -15 comes from. The
“militia” clause confuses her the way it confuses me

23

and millions of other Americans . This Court should
pronounce the “militia” clause extinct and hold that
its extinction means that the operative clause  is for
individual self-defense and hunting for food. It means
that the Second Amendment gives people the right to
keep and bear arms reasonably necessary for self -
defense and hunting . That is where the Second
Amendment right “stops and the State's authority to
regulate begins.”  United States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S.
680, 737 (2024) (Barrett, J., concurring). Congress ,
states, counties, and municipalities can ban, limit, or
allow deadlier arms . Respondents limit deadlier
arms.
CONCLUSION
The Second and Fourteenth Amendments to the
United States Constitution do not guarantee the right
to possess semiautomatic rifles that are in common
use for lawful purposes, including the most popular
rifle in the country, the AR -15. The judgments of the
Second and Seventh Circuits should be affirmed.
